output.title: Check data residency before you automate
output.body:
Before you automate a workflow, make data residency the first control, not a footnote. By residency, I mean where the data is allowed to sit and move: on your own systems, in a specific country, or inside a vendor service. For an owner-operator, the real question is not “can AI do this?” but “which parts of this workflow are allowed to leave my environment at all?”

Take one recurring process you already do by hand, such as customer-data entry, invoice processing, or lead follow-up. Treat it as an example only, not a customer case. List the fields that are sensitive, contract-bound, or just not meant for a third party: payment details, personal data, internal pricing, or anything a supplier agreement keeps in place. Then read the tool’s own service terms and data-handling docs. Bareni does not offer compliance or security guarantees here; the vendor’s documentation is what matters.

If most of the workflow can move, a pilot may make sense. If the whole workflow must stay local, you are looking at a self-hosted or tightly integrated approach. That is the useful boundary: what can move, and what must stay put. Slightly less glamorous than a launch video, but more useful on Monday.
